items.title: William Russell Interview, 1976-02-16
items.q: There was Kepard, I guess, probably couldn't read anything at all.

ctx.x: Panorama, it was in the panorama that he edited. I don't know where the original was. It's a very good article, I thought. What's always interested me was this use of the word legitimate. And I know you're a classical musician as well.

Yeah, a lot of other people. In fact, Jelly used that term too. I was talking about violin players, which Jelly didn't use hardly ever, as far as I know he did use on one of his records, Someday Sweetheart. But he evidently didn't look with too much favor on violins. He said even in New Orleans, the statement was he never heard any illegitimate. He called it the violin players. They were all legitimate, more or less straight players. That's usually the reason they would have them in a band too. Not maybe the main…
Of course, there's a popular, of course, there's also the assumption that the jazz musician is better who can't read.

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1962-09-04
items.q: but Kepford was his favorite trumpet player

ctx.x: I have a note here. He mentioned that there were

three great clarinetists in New Orleans. Piku, Lorenzo Tio, and George Bakke. He didn't think Big Eye Louie was really in the first class. Other people will tell you they think Big Eye was better than Piku and so on. So some of that could be a question of opinion. he thought Dodds wasn't really a first class clarinetist. He was all right. He was only on a couple of his records, maybe four sides or so. I don't know. I even asked him once, I said, is it true that Muggsy had recorded with him? And he said, yes. No,…
He was dead in that two summer.

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1975-02-02
items.q: It's loud as Keppard or Wooden Joe or people like that.

ctx.x: So anyway, to get back to the point, Gene Williams had heard these records and agreed with me too that at least Bunk showed some possibilities. You couldn't really tell much how he played, both because his lip wasn't in shape and just by himself. The type of trumpet playing that Bunk did, which was a remarkable thing, and yet by itself it wouldn't sound that effective. Bunk was hardly ever on the beat, so if you didn't hear him patting his foot and all there, you could really tell of course where the beat is, but…
Well, of course, we'll never know what Joe Oliver really sounded like.

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1962-08-31
items.q: Almost all the members of that band except Freddie Keppert at that time were living.

ctx.x: Well, maybe you could correct him.

A footnote or something like that. Yes, sort of evaluate some of that, too. I'd rather do that and not take a lot of time on the tape now to do that. And they're not in a condition to be photostadded or Xerox or whatever it is. Another man who's dead now, Buddy Christian, an outstanding banjo and guitar player from New Orleans, who also played piano here and also in New York. And he played on quite a few of the Clarence Williams Hot Five. And what are they called? Blue Five, excuse me. Anyway, he's been dead for…
